package_info.why_malicious: The affected versions of Spring Framework contain a critical vulnerability (CVE-2022-22965) that allows remote attackers to manipulate internal ClassLoader attributes via HTTP POST parameter binding. This enables attackers to reconfigure Tomcat's logging pipeline and write arbitrary files, such as web shells, to web-accessible directories, resulting in unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) on the server.

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when a vulnerable Spring Web Controller endpoint receives an HTTP POST request with specially crafted parameters.
execution_context.file_location: Any Spring Web Controller endpoint that binds POST parameters to Java POJOs (Plain Old Java Objects).
required_permissions: filesystem (to write files to web-accessible directories)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when a vulnerable Spring endpoint receives a crafted HTTP POST request, the code binds attacker-supplied parameters to internal Tomcat logging configuration, reconfigures the logging pipeline to write a .jsp file containing attacker-controlled code to the web root, and enables remote code execution when the file is accessed.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The POST parameters directly manipulate internal Tomcat logging configuration, allowing an external attacker to write arbitrary files (such as web shells) to the server's web root. This is a clear remote code execution pattern, as it enables the attacker to deploy and execute malicious code remotely.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal POST parameter binding in Spring should only map user input to application-level business objects, not expose or allow modification of internal server configuration or file system paths. Here, user input is mapped to sensitive server internals, violating the principle of least privilege and application isolation.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate use of POST parameter binding is limited to mapping user input to application data models (POJOs) for business logic processing. There is no legitimate scenario where user-supplied parameters should alter Tomcat's logging configuration or write files to the web root.
key_indicators: Presence of POST parameters prefixed with class.module.classLoader.*
Modification of Tomcat pipeline attributes (e.g., .suffix, .directory, .pattern) via HTTP request
Creation of .jsp files in web-accessible directories (e.g., webapps/ROOT/)
Pattern parameter containing executable code (e.g., web shell payloads)
Absence of authentication or authorization checks on sensitive parameter binding

attack_chain.action: Attacker identifies a POST endpoint in a Spring application that binds request parameters to POJOs, exposing the application to parameter binding attacks.
attack_chain.leads_to: Ability to send crafted POST requests to vulnerable endpoints

attack_chain.action: Attacker sends a crafted HTTP POST request with parameters that reconfigure Tomcat's logging pipeline to write a .jsp file containing malicious code to a web-accessible directory.
attack_chain.leads_to: Arbitrary file write of a web shell to the server's web root

attack_chain.action: Attacker accesses the newly created .jsp file via HTTP, causing the server to execute the attacker's code and granting remote code execution.
attack_chain.leads_to: Remote code execution (RCE) on the server

behavioral_signatures: HTTP POST requests to Spring endpoints containing parameters prefixed with class.module.classLoader.*
Unexpected runtime changes to Tomcat logging configuration (e.g., pipeline.first.* attributes)
Creation of new .jsp files in web-accessible directories (such as webapps/ROOT/) without corresponding deployment events
file_indicators: webapps/ROOT/*.jsp files created or modified outside of normal deployment processes
Log files or web root files with .jsp extension containing web shell code patterns (e.g., code that executes arbitrary commands via HTTP parameters)
network_indicators: Unusual HTTP POST requests to Spring endpoints with suspicious parameter names (class.module.classLoader.*)
Subsequent HTTP GET requests to newly created .jsp files in the web root, especially from external IPs
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor HTTP POST requests for parameters such as class.module.classLoader.resources.context.parent.pipeline.first.*. Alert on the creation or modification of .jsp files in web-accessible directories (e.g., webapps/ROOT/) outside of normal deployment. Correlate suspicious HTTP activity with file creation events and review Tomcat runtime configuration changes. Use web shell pattern matching to scan new .jsp files for malicious payloads.
